abstract: The BLS Employment Projections program's first official occupational AI exposure classification, published to complement the 2025-35 employment projections. Rather than producing a new exposure measure, BLS combines five existing external measures into a single four-category relative ranking (Low, Moderate, High, Very high) covering every detailed occupation for which projections are produced. Three inputs are theoretical measures that score how well AI capabilities match the work an occupation performs: Felten, Raj and Seamans (mTurk survey respondents rating whether 10 AI applications relate to occupational abilities), Eloundou, Manning, Mishkin and Rock (whether an LLM could cut task time by at least half, human and GPT-4 ratings), and Eisfeldt, Schubert, Taska and Zhang (the Eloundou framework applied to O*NET tasks via GPT-3.5 Turbo). Two inputs are observed-usage measures: Anthropic (Massenkoff and McCrory), which maps Claude.ai conversations and API traffic to O*NET tasks and weights tasks with relatively higher automative than augmentative use more heavily, and Microsoft (Tomlinson, Jaffe, Wang, Counts and Suri), which maps observed Copilot usage to O*NET Intermediate Work Activities using GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini and GPT-5. BLS maps each source to the 2018 SOC, converts each occupation's score to a percentile rank within its source to put all five on a common 0-1 scale, takes the median percentile rank across the three theoretical sources and separately across the two observed sources, and runs a clustering algorithm over those two dimensions to assign the four categories. The framing is deliberately relative and deliberately not predictive: BLS states the categories are not a forecast of employment, wages, adoption probability, worker replacement, or productivity, and do not distinguish automation from augmentation.
keyFindings: BLS created four relative AI exposure categories — Low, Moderate, High, Very high — for every detailed occupation in the 2025-35 projections, its first official occupational AI exposure product. The categories are relative to other occupations and do not imply an absolute high or low level of exposure.

The classification combines five external sources: three theoretical (Felten/Raj/Seamans; Eloundou/Manning/Mishkin/Rock; Eisfeldt/Schubert/Taska/Zhang) and two observed-usage (Anthropic's Claude-based measure from Massenkoff and McCrory; Microsoft's Copilot-based measure from Tomlinson et al.). BLS notes the three theoretical sources 'do not all measure equivalent concepts.'

Method: each occupation's score is converted to a percentile rank within its source, placing all five measures on a common 0-1 scale and converting raw values into relative ones. BLS then takes the median percentile rank across the three theoretical sources and across the two observed sources, and clusters occupations on those two dimensions.

Coverage: 831 occupations times 5 sources = 4,155 possible occupation-source combinations. 3,944 were observed and 211 were imputed, affecting 75 occupations. Imputation predicts a missing rank from the other available sources and the occupation's two-digit SOC major group.

BLS states explicitly that an exposure category is not a forecast of employment growth or decline, not a wage forecast, not an estimate of AI adoption probability, not a worker replacement estimate, and not a productivity forecast. 'High' or 'Very high' exposure does not necessarily mean employment will decline, and 'Low' does not mean an occupation is safe from future technological change.

Measurement limits are dated: the three theoretical sources conceptualize AI capabilities as those available no later than mid-2023, the observed sources may lean toward early adopters of specific models, and most sources focus on language modeling only, excluding image and video generation. All five treat occupations as bundles of independent characteristics and ignore bottlenecks and complementarities.
methodology: Meta-analytic classification rather than original measurement. BLS crosswalks five external occupational AI exposure measures to the 2018 Standard Occupational Classification used by the Employment Projections program, normalizes each via within-source percentile rank (0-1), imputes missing values from other available sources plus two-digit SOC major group, computes two composite dimensions (median percentile rank across three theoretical sources; median across two observed-usage sources), then applies a clustering algorithm over those two dimensions to produce four categories. A supplemental table pairs the categories with the 2025-35 employment projections and is published as a downloadable XLSX. Projections are produced annually; the 2026-36 round is scheduled for release in 2027.
qualifiers: Tier 1 — US government statistical agency, fully documented method, downloadable data. The essential caveat is that this is a relative ranking, not a level: it produces no economy-wide 'share of jobs exposed' figure and cannot be read as one. BLS is unusually explicit that the categories forecast nothing — not employment, wages, adoption, replacement, or productivity — and do not separate automation from augmentation. The inputs are also dated: theoretical measures are pinned to AI capabilities available no later than mid-2023, so frontier capability gains since then are not reflected. Observed-usage inputs come from two vendors (Anthropic, Microsoft) whose user bases may skew toward early adopters, and they measure AI interaction mapped to tasks rather than direct observation of whether workers in an occupation actually used AI. Imputation touches 75 of 831 occupations. Because three of the five inputs are already ingested as standalone sources on this site, this source should be treated as superseding rather than supplementing them for any aggregate exposure claim.
